results.title: The lack of statistical power of subgroup analyses in meta-analyses: a cautionary note
results.content: One of the most used methods to examine sources of heterogeneity in meta-analyses is the so-called ‘subgroup analysis’. We show that subgroup analyses require many more included studies in a meta-analysis than are needed for the main analyses. We work out an example of an ‘average’ meta-analysis, in which a subgroup analysis requires 3–4 times the number of studies that are needed for the main analysis to have sufficient power. The second author of this paper recently developed _metapower_, a statistical package in R for conducting power analyses for general meta-analyses (e.g., summary effect size) and subgroup analyses (Griffin, 2021). A simple example can show that you need many more studies to detect subgroup differences than you would need to detect a main effect in the meta-analysis. For such a subgroup analysis, a total of 22 studies would be needed to have 80% power, almost four times the number of studies needed for the main analyses. ### Varying subgroup differences The number of studies needed for subgroup analyses increases exponentially when the difference in effect sizes between the subgroups gets smaller. For small subgroup differences (e.g., SMD=0.1), the number of studies required is 83 times that needed for the main analysis. In Fig. 1 we graphically present the number of studies needed in different scenarios for subgroup analyses. Open in a new tab Number of studies needed in subgroup analyses within meta-analyses for 80% power, depending on the difference between the effect sizes of the subgroups and the proportion of studies in each subgroup. In our hypothetical meta-analysis (50 participants per study, _I_ 2=50%, SMD between the two subgroups of 0.5) we need 22 studies for 80% power, but 28 for 90% power. For example, when heterogeneity is low (_I_ 2=25%) and the studies are evenly divided over the subgroups, 14 studies are needed for detecting an SMD between the subgroups of 0.5, more than twice the number for the main meta-analysis of our hypothetical example. Power calculations indicate that subgroup analyses in a meta-analysis require dozens to hundreds of studies for realising sufficient statistical power.

For information about the n-sizes included in state ESSA plans approved by the U.S. Department of Education, see the following, more recent All4Ed publications*:. Publication | Accountability and Support, Data, Every Student Succeeds Act. ### N-Size in ESSA State Plans. All4Ed’s analysis of the minimum number of students in a school, or n-size, states chose for their school accountability systems and report cards under ESSA. ### Ensuring Every Student Matters What Is N-Size and Why Is It Important? How do states set the minimum number of students needed to form a subgroup and what does that mean for monitoring outcomes of historically underserved students? All4Ed’s ESSA Equity Dashboards use a red-yellow-green light–system to rate each state’s ESSA plan on several indicators, including long-term goals, accountability indicators, and school ratings. #### Ensuring Equity in ESSA: The Role of N-Size in Subgroup Accountability. States are responsible for setting the minimum number of students needed to form a student subgroup for federal reporting and school accountability purposes. This required student subgroup size is commonly referred to as the state-set “n-size.”. This report recommends states set their n-size as low as possible (ten or fewer students) to maximize the number of student subgroups created. This will ensure states identify student subgroups with low academic performance and/or low high school graduation rates and provide targeted interventions to support the schools those students attend. Specifically, states should not require a subgroup to include more than ten students in order to include that subgroup for reporting and accountability purposes. In addition, All4Ed more than thirty civil rights, disability, and data-focused organizations sent a letter urging the U.S. Department of Education to decrease its proposed n-size threshold from thirty to ten in the final ESSA accountability regulations. ## Pop-Up Modal Lorem Ipsum Dolor Sit Amet. results.title: Advanced Subgroup Analysis Techniques
results.content: Traditional subgroup analysis techniques have limitations, and recent advancements in machine learning and Bayesian methods have opened up new avenues for more accurate and reliable results. In this article, we will explore the latest developments in subgroup analysis, including the application of machine learning and Bayesian techniques, and discuss their advantages and challenges. ## Machine Learning for Subgroup Analysis. Machine learning techniques have been widely applied in subgroup analysis, particularly in the context of patient stratification and outcome prediction. ### Challenges and Limitations of Machine Learning in Subgroup Analysis. While machine learning techniques have shown great promise in subgroup analysis, there are several challenges and limitations that need to be addressed. ## Bayesian Methods for Subgroup Analysis. Bayesian methods offer a flexible and robust approach to subgroup analysis, allowing researchers to model complex relationships and incorporate prior knowledge. ### Applications of Bayesian Methods in Subgroup Analysis. Bayesian methods have been widely applied in subgroup analysis, particularly in the context of modeling uncertainty and incorporating prior knowledge. * **Incorporating Prior Knowledge**: Bayesian methods can be used to incorporate prior knowledge into subgroup analysis, allowing researchers to update their beliefs based on new data. ### Advantages and Challenges of Bayesian Methods in Subgroup Analysis. Bayesian methods offer several advantages in subgroup analysis, including the ability to model complex relationships and incorporate prior knowledge. Machine learning and Bayesian methods are both powerful tools for subgroup analysis, but they have different strengths and weaknesses. Subgroup analysis is a critical aspect of research in various fields, and recent advancements in machine learning and Bayesian methods have opened up new avenues for more accurate and reliable results. ### What are the limitations of using Bayesian methods for subgroup analysis? ### How do I choose between machine learning and Bayesian methods for subgroup analysis? Machine learning is suitable for exploratory subgroup analysis, while Bayesian methods are suitable for confirmatory subgroup analysis. ### Can I use both machine learning and Bayesian methods for subgroup analysis? Yes, it is possible to use both machine learning and Bayesian methods for subgroup analysis. For example, machine learning can be used for exploratory subgroup analysis, and Bayesian methods can be used for confirmatory subgroup analysis.

results.content: Best Practices for Determining Subgroup Size in Accountability Systems While Protecting Personally Identifiable Student Information | IES Homearrow_forward_iosResource Library Searcharrow_forward_ios Best Practices for Determining Subg ... Best Practices for Determining Subgroup Size in Accountability Systems While Protecting Personally Identifiable Student Information SSDCS - Statistical Standards and Data Confidentiality Staff The Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) of 2015 (Public Law 114-95) requires each state to create a plan for its statewide accountability system. In their plans, states must specify a single value for the minimum number of students needed to provide statistically sound data for all students and for each subgroup, while protecting personally identifiable information (PII) of individual students. For example, the selection of smaller minimum n-sizes will ensure that more students' outcomes are included in a state's accountability system, but smaller n-sizes can also increase the likelihood of the inadvertent disclosure of PII. Similarly, smaller minimum n-sizes enable more complete data to be reported, but they may also affect the reliability and statistical validity of the data. To inform this complex decision, Congress required the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) of the U.S. Department of Education to produce and widely disseminate a report on "best practices for determining valid, reliable, and statistically significant minimum numbers of students for each of the subgroups of students" (Every Student Succeeds Act of 2015 (ESSA 2015), Public Law 114-95). Congress also directed that the report describe how such a minimum number "will not reveal personally identifiable information about students." ESSA prohibits IES from recommending any specific minimum number of students in a subgroup (Section 9209). IES produced this report to assist states as they develop accountability systems that (1) comply with ESSA; (2) incorporate sound statistical practices and protections; and (3) meet the information needs of state accountability reporting, while still protecting the privacy of individual students. As presented in this report, the minimum n-size refers to the lowest statistically defensible subgroup size that can be reported in a state accountability system. Before getting started, it is important to understand that the minimum n-size a state establishes and the privacy protections it implements will directly determine how much data will be publicly reported in the system.
